scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The farruca emerged as a flamenco form in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Its origins are uncertain, though it is often linked to Galician folklore.
It was solidified as a theatrical dance and guitar piece in 1908 by the dancer Faíco and guitarist Ramón Montoya.
on_screen: Map: Spain · Europe
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Traditionally a theatrical solo, it is performed in stage settings and concert halls.
It represents sobriety, authority, and masculine-coded defiance, though these meanings have been expanded by modern female interpreters.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Men Dancing 10 (https://archive.org/details/csfpal_000160)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is characterized by upright, proud posture, sharp zapateado (footwork), and dramatic pauses.
It follows a binary 4/4 meter with accents on the 1st, 3rd, 5th, and 7th beats.
It includes fast turns, held poses, and extended footwork sections called escobillas.
Watch for Zapateado, Llamada.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (3j5IRvgQAS8)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Solo performance, utilizing stage space for dramatic entrances and exits.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Performed primarily in A minor, the music uses a binary meter.
Guitar accompaniment often alternates between E7 and A minor.
Listen for the Guitar.
The pulse is 4/4.
A sober, minor-key sound dominated by the guitar, characterized by a steady, driving rhythmic pulse and sharp, percussive accents that emphasize the dancer's footwork.
